Tennessee enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament at 22-11 overall and 11-7 in SEC play, with a fourth-place league finish listed by ESPN after the SEC Tournament semifinal loss to Vanderbilt on March 13, 2026. The Vols closed the regular season 21-10, then beat Auburn 72-62 in the SEC quarterfinals before losing 75-68 to Vanderbilt in Nashville, giving them the final 22-11 mark on Selection Week. Their statistical profile is clear and specific: through 33 games, Tennessee averaged 79.5 points, 42.6 rebounds, 16.9 assists and 7.5 steals per game while allowing 69.4 points per game; ESPN lists Ja’Kobi Gillespie as the team leader at 18.0 points and 5.5 assists per game, Nate Ament at 17.5 points and 6.6 rebounds, and Felix Okpara at 1.4 blocks per game. Tennessee’s team identity is also unusually concrete on the glass: Sports-Reference shows 16.0 offensive rebounds per game, and Tennessee game notes in late January stated the Vols led the nation in offensive rebounding percentage at 43.9 percent and had recorded double-digit offensive boards in 18 of 19 games at that point. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/schedule/_/id/2633/season/2026))

Offensively, this is not a spread-isolation team living on volume threes. The shot distribution shows that: Sports-Reference credits Tennessee with only 6.6 made threes per game, but 22.0 made twos and the nation’s No. 1 offensive rebounding rate. That points directly to a Barnes offense built around paint touches, second shots, and guard-to-big creation rather than bombing away. Specific evidence backs that up. Against Georgia on January 28, Tennessee survived poor first-half shooting by creating a 15-3 offensive-rebound edge before halftime and finished the night with a 26-7 offensive-glass margin. Against Texas A&M on January 13, the Vols posted 60 rebounds, an SEC-game high noted by Tennessee. Against South Carolina State on December 30, Tennessee recorded 30 assists on 39 made field goals, with Ja’Kobi Gillespie posting eight assists and Bishop Boswell and Troy Henderson six each, showing the other side of the offense: when the ball pops, they can play through multiple handlers and hit cutters. In practical scouting terms, Tennessee’s favorite offensive actions are guard-led ball-screen offense for Gillespie, elbow and high-post touches for Ament, and relentless crash patterns from Carey, Estrella, Okpara and Ament. The results show up in named games: Gillespie had 34 points, five assists, four rebounds and three steals against Texas on January 6; Ament had 29 at Alabama on January 24 and 29 more versus Oklahoma on February 18; and Carey’s putback with 1:14 left in the second overtime against Texas A&M was a classic Tennessee possession won by second effort. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/tennessee/men/2026.html?utm_source=openai))

Defensively, Tennessee still looks like Rick Barnes basketball: heavy ball pressure, physical half-court defense, and an obsession with making opponents finish over size. The numbers are concrete. Sports-Reference lists opponents at 41.1 percent from the field, 30.8 percent from three, only 29.3 rebounds per game, and 10.7 assists per game against Tennessee. That rebounding suppression matters because it ends possessions and fuels the Vols’ transition and early offense. There is also documented scheme flexibility. A February Tennessee press-clips packet quoting DeWayne Brown after the Vanderbilt win said, “We changed our ball screen coverage,” and explained that Tennessee used less hard hedge and more drop coverage because Vanderbilt was slipping the hedge to create advantage. That is not abstract philosophy; it is a named in-season coverage adjustment. Tennessee also held Auburn on January 31 to 38.1 percent shooting and 22.6 percent from three, even though Auburn entered that game No. 10 nationally in KenPom adjusted offensive efficiency. When the Vols are right, they squeeze airspace, finish possessions, and force opponents into late-clock jumpers. ([sports-reference.com](https://www.sports-reference.com/cbb/schools/tennessee/men/2026.html?utm_source=openai))

Barnes’ coaching philosophy remains veteran and possession-driven: defend first, rebound violently, trust experienced guards, and do not give away soft points. But the 2025-26 season also shows a coach still willing to adjust. The Georgia game on January 28 is the cleanest in-game example. Tennessee trailed 34-28 at halftime after shooting just 31.4 percent and 18.2 percent from three in the first half, then scored 46 after halftime and won 86-85 in overtime. That is a documented game where Barnes’ team corrected shot quality and execution midstream. The Vanderbilt road win on February 21 provides the defensive version: Tennessee altered ball-screen coverage and held the Commodores to 33 points over the final 25 minutes, per the clip package. On the other hand, the Kentucky games show Barnes’ group has not always protected leads: Tennessee blew a 17-point first-half lead in an 80-78 home loss on January 17, then led 28-18 in Lexington on February 7 before falling 74-71. So the adjustment history is mixed but specific: Barnes can find counters, yet his team has still had trouble landing games against elite shot-makers. ([utsports.com](https://utsports.com/news/2026/1/28/mens-basketball-vols-notch-86-85-overtime-triumph-at-georgia-for-barnes-850th-victory?utm_source=openai))

Clutch and late-game execution is the swing category for this team. Tennessee has several positive close-game examples. On January 13 against Texas A&M, the Vols won 87-82 in double overtime; in the second extra session, Carey scored the putback with 1:14 left, Ament hit two free throws with 12.7 seconds left, and Tennessee did not allow another point after Jacari Lane cut it to 84-82 with 15.8 seconds remaining. On January 24 at Alabama, Tennessee answered a Crimson Tide push with seven of the next nine points to rebuild a two-possession lead and won 79-73. On January 28 at Georgia, Tennessee won 86-85 in overtime after trailing by six at halftime. On February 21 at No. 19 Vanderbilt, the Vols won 69-65 for their second AP top-20 road win of the season. But the negative file is real: January 17 versus Kentucky, Tennessee led by 17 and lost 80-78; February 7 at Kentucky, Tennessee led 28-18 and lost 74-71; February 28 versus Alabama, Tennessee led 67-61 with 3:41 left and still lost 71-69 after Labaron Philon Jr. scored six straight to tie it; and March 7 versus Vanderbilt, Tennessee lost 86-82 at home. This is a team capable of winning grind games, but not one you would call automatic in the final four minutes. ([utsports.com](https://utsports.com/news/2026/1/13/mens-basketball-24-rv-vols-upend-texas-am-87-82-in-double-overtime-thriller))

The key players are easy to identify and each has a defined job. Gillespie is the engine: 18.0 points, 5.5 assists and 2.1 steals per game on ESPN, with signature scoring games of 34 against Texas on January 6, 32 against Rutgers on November 24, 26 against Alabama on February 28, and 21 in the SEC Tournament loss to Vanderbilt on March 13. He is the late-clock ball-handler and best perimeter creator. Ament is the matchup problem: 17.5 points and 6.6 rebounds per game, with 29 at Alabama on January 24, 29 against Kentucky on February 7, 28 versus Ole Miss on February 3, 29 versus Oklahoma on February 18, and 27 in the SEC Tournament win over Auburn on March 12. Estrella gives them interior scoring pop off the frontcourt rotation; he scored 22 at South Carolina on March 3 and had 23 versus North Florida on November 12. Okpara supplies rim protection and efficient finishing, averaging 7.7 points, 6.2 rebounds and 1.4 blocks; he had 20 against Rice on November 17 and 12 rebounds in the double-overtime win over Texas A&M. Carey is the glass-and-contact forward, averaging 10.1 points and 5.2 rebounds in 17.7 minutes, with the decisive late putback against Texas A&M and multiple 10-rebound games. Boswell matters as the connective piece: 6.2 points, 4.5 rebounds and 2.9 assists, including eight assists at Mississippi State on February 11. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/stats/_/id/2633/sort/gamesPlayed))

The notable wins tell you Tennessee’s ceiling. Beating Houston 76-73 on November 25 was an early signal that the Vols could handle elite physicality. Winning at Alabama 79-73 on January 24 showed they could beat a high-end offense on the road, with Ament scoring 29. Beating Auburn 77-69 on January 31 showed the defensive ceiling, because Tennessee held an offense rated No. 10 in KenPom efficiency to 38.1 percent overall and 22.6 percent from three. The 72-62 SEC Tournament win over Auburn on March 12 reinforced that Tennessee can still win a rock fight against a top seed. The losses reveal the vulnerability: Kansas 81-76 on November 26 and Illinois 75-62 on December 6 suggested Tennessee can be stressed by teams with shot-making size; Florida’s 91-67 win on January 10 exposed them when the game gets too fast; both Kentucky losses showed late-game leakage; and Alabama’s 71-69 win on February 28 showed that even after building a six-point lead inside four minutes, Tennessee can still get undone by shot creation and one missed execution sequence. ([espn.com](https://www.espn.com/mens-college-basketball/team/schedule/_/id/2633/season/2026))

Barnes’ NCAA Tournament history is extensive and relevant. Tennessee’s official bio says he led the Vols to back-to-back Elite Eight trips in 2024 and 2025, and Tennessee’s March 2025 NCAA release states the program was 9-6 in NCAA Tournament games under Barnes at that time, the most tournament wins by any coach in school history. More broadly, Tennessee’s historical page says 2024 was the program’s second-ever Elite Eight, while Barnes’ Tennessee bio notes he has taken the Vols to four Sweet 16s and two Elite Eights during the current run. Across his whole career, Barnes has made 29 NCAA Tournaments entering 2025-26, with a Final Four at Texas in 2003, multiple Sweet 16 runs, and now consecutive Elite Eight appearances at Tennessee in 2024 and 2025. For this specific Tennessee team, that matters because Barnes has recently proven he can take a defense-first roster deep into March; the question is whether this group’s uneven late-game execution can hold up for six straight possessions against tournament-level guards. ([utsports.com](https://utsports.com/sports/mens-basketball/roster/coaches/rick-barnes/5377?utm_source=openai))

Tennessee enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament with a profile that is strong by predictive metrics, but more complicated in its statistical texture than the program’s usual national reputation. Broadly, the Volunteers look like a clear top-20 team by the major systems, with most of the available evidence clustering them in the back half of the top 20 rather than on the true top-line contender tier. KenPom lists Tennessee 16th nationally with a +25.98 adjusted efficiency margin, built from a 121.0 adjusted offensive efficiency and a 95.1 adjusted defensive efficiency. That defensive figure ranks 15th nationally, while the offense ranks 34th. ESPN’s BPI places Tennessee 12th nationally, with offensive and defensive components of +8.7 and +10.2 respectively. The NCAA’s public NET board is harder to extract cleanly from the page snapshot, but Tennessee was explicitly cited as 21st in NET in early February, while also 18th in KenPom at that point, indicating a team that improved some in predictive standing by Selection Week even if its resume ranking never screamed top-eight seed quality. ([kenpom.com](https://kenpom.com/))

That split is central to understanding Tennessee. This is not the classic Rick Barnes Tennessee team that wins primarily by suffocating defense and half-court grind while dragging an inconsistent offense along for the ride. The 2025-26 Vols are still good defensively, but the predictive systems suggest a more balanced profile with the offense actually carrying more weight than public perception might assume. KenPom’s 121.0 adjusted offense versus 95.1 adjusted defense implies a team that is very good on both ends, but slightly more dangerous offensively than the eye test might suggest, especially because Tennessee’s raw shooting efficiency does not immediately look elite. ([kenpom.com](https://kenpom.com/))

On the surface stat line, Tennessee’s offense is productive without looking aesthetically dominant. In the March 3 game notes, the Vols were scoring 80.1 points per game, allowing 69.2, and posting a 10.9 scoring margin. Their team effective field-goal percentage was 52.0 percent, which ranked just 175th nationally at that snapshot, while their raw field-goal percentage was 46.5 percent and three-point percentage was 34.3 percent. Earlier checkpoints show the same pattern: on January 24 they owned a 54.1 percent eFG, and by February 3 they sat at 53.5 percent. That downward drift into early March is meaningful. This is a good offense, but not because it bombs teams from deep or because it posts an overwhelming shot-making profile. ([utsports.com](https://utsports.com/documents/download/2026/3/2/G30_3-3-26_South_Carolina.pdf))

Instead, Tennessee’s offensive identity is built on volume edges. The best evidence is on the glass and at the foul line. In early February, the Vols were averaging 15.7 offensive rebounds per game, second nationally, with 43.1 total rebounds per game and a +12.8 rebound margin, both fourth nationally. Tennessee’s own notes also state that the team led the nation in offensive rebounding percentage at 45.0 percent in early January, and an outside Tennessee analysis citing KenPom described the Vols’ offensive rebounding margin as 46.1, best in the country. That is a massive structural advantage: Tennessee creates extra possessions at an elite rate, which helps explain why a merely decent shooting team can still grade as a top-35 offense. ([olemisssports.com](https://olemisssports.com/documents/download/2026/2/2/22_-_Tennessee.pdf))

Using available team totals and rate stats, Tennessee’s underlying possession-profile looks like this: three-point attempt rate is about 34.0 percent, based on 19.7 threes attempted per game out of an estimated 57.9 total field-goal attempts per game; free-throw rate is about 41.1 percent, based on 23.8 free-throw attempts per game over the same estimated shot volume; offensive rebounding rate is about 36.4 percent using the team’s 15.7 offensive and 27.4 defensive rebounds per game snapshot; and turnover rate is roughly 17.5 percent if you pair 12.5 turnovers per game with an estimated 71.3 possessions. None of those are exact official possession-based rates, but they are directionally useful and align with what the rest of the evidence says: Tennessee does not lean into extreme perimeter volume, does get to the stripe a lot, and absolutely hammers the offensive glass. ([utsports.com](https://utsports.com/documents/download/2026/3/2/G30_3-3-26_South_Carolina.pdf))

The defensive profile is cleaner and more in line with conventional Barnes-era expectations. Tennessee ranked first in the SEC in scoring defense and three-point percentage defense, while placing 32nd nationally in field-goal percentage defense and 32nd nationally in three-point defense by the March 3 snapshot. Earlier, on February 3, the Vols were allowing just 39.9 percent from the field and 29.4 percent from three. KenPom’s 95.1 adjusted defensive efficiency and BPI’s defensive component both confirm that this is a genuine top-15-to-top-20 defense nationally, even if not the absolute top-five unit some observers may reflexively assume when they hear “Tennessee.” ([utsports.com](https://utsports.com/documents/download/2026/3/2/G30_3-3-26_South_Carolina.pdf))

Pace is slow. KenPom lists Tennessee at 65.0 adjusted tempo, 307th nationally, which is one of the most important tournament-context indicators on the profile. This team plays a reduced-possession game, which raises variance in March and can keep weaker opponents alive if Tennessee’s offensive rebounding edge is neutralized. ESPN’s BPI page does not publish tempo the same way, but nothing in the available raw data contradicts the KenPom read: Tennessee is methodical, physical, and possession-oriented rather than transition-heavy. ([kenpom.com](https://kenpom.com/))

Schedule strength appears solid rather than overwhelming. KenPom’s schedule column on the Tennessee line shows the Vols with a schedule strength figure ranked 11th nationally, which is excellent. ESPN’s BPI page also lists Tennessee’s remaining SOS rank at 48th on the captured page, but that is a forward-looking remainder metric rather than full-season SOS. The résumé itself included notable nonconference wins over Rutgers, Houston, and Louisville by early February, which supports the idea that Tennessee was tested against real tournament-caliber competition. ([kenpom.com](https://kenpom.com/))

Recent form was mixed heading into the bracket. Tennessee had won three straight entering the Ole Miss game on February 3, including wins at Alabama, at Georgia, and over Auburn, but the closing stretch included losses to Alabama on February 28, Vanderbilt on March 7, a win over Auburn in the SEC tournament on March 12, and another loss to Vanderbilt on March 13. That is not a collapse, but it does suggest some late volatility rather than a clean upward trend over the final 10 games. The offense’s decline in eFG from 54.1 in late January to 53.5 in early February to 52.0 by early March is a useful proxy for that drift: Tennessee remained efficient overall because of rebounding and free throws, but the shot-making trend was not obviously peaking at the right time. ([rolltide.com](https://rolltide.com/documents/download/2026/1/23/G19_1-24-26_Alabama.pdf))

Where the numbers diverge from conventional wisdom is this: Tennessee “looks” like a defense-first grinder, but the actual statistical profile says the team’s distinguishing tournament trait is offensive possession creation. The Vols are not elite by eFG%, not especially high-volume from three, and not a fast team. Yet they still post top-35 offensive efficiency because they punish opponents on the glass and manufacture free throws. Conversely, the defense is very good, but not quite the generational unit that the brand name might imply. Put simply: this Tennessee team wins more with second shots and physicality than with perimeter shot-making brilliance, and more with balance than with an overwhelming defense-only identity. That makes them dangerous, but also somewhat matchup-sensitive. Opponents that can end possessions cleanly, limit fouls, and force Tennessee to win purely on first-shot half-court offense have the clearest upset blueprint. ([kenpom.com](https://kenpom.com/))
matchup-analyst:
Tennessee enters the 2026 NCAA Tournament as a defense-and-glass driven team whose identity is more physical than pretty. Through 22 games in the official Tennessee game notes, the Vols were scoring 82.2 points per game, allowing 69.6, shooting 47.6 percent overall, holding opponents to 40.0 percent, and ranking No. 2 in the SEC in 3-point defense at 29.7 percent. The most important style marker is on the offensive glass: Tennessee’s own game notes state the Vols led the nation in KenPom offensive rebounding percentage at 45.2 percent as of early February, and they had reached double-digit offensive rebounds in 21 of 22 games. ([utsports.com](https://utsports.com/documents/download/2026/2/5/G23_2-7-26_Kentucky.pdf))

That tells you the base style: half-court defense, long athletes, pressure on the rim via second chances, and enough shot-making from Ja’Kobi Gillespie and Nate Ament to survive slower possessions. Gillespie was at 18.6 points and 119 assists through 22 games, while Ament was at 17.1 points and 6.4 rebounds; those are the two primary offensive problem-solvers. Tennessee is not a high-volume 3-point attack team, however. Through 22 games it was making only 7.2 threes per game and attempting 20.5, both 15th in the SEC. So the disruption formula is specific: take away their extra possessions, make them finish over a set half-court defense, and force role players rather than Gillespie/Ament to create late-clock offense. ([utsports.com](https://utsports.com/documents/download/2026/2/5/G23_2-7-26_Kentucky.pdf))

The clearest tactical way to bother Tennessee is to win the turnover-possession battle before the rebounding advantage shows up. In the 91-67 loss at Florida on January 10, 2026, Tennessee was outscored 18-6 in points off turnovers and never recovered from Florida’s late first-half 15-2 burst. That game also shows what happens when Tennessee cannot dominate the glass enough to offset giveaways: the Vols managed only six offensive rebounds, their season low at that point, and only 30 total rebounds, also a season low in the game notes. ([utsports.com](https://utsports.com/news/2026/1/10/mens-basketball-21-22-vols-fall-on-the-road-at-florida))

Press and zone vulnerability are real enough to target, though not because Tennessee collapses automatically against either. The better evidence is that compact, help-heavy defenses that make Tennessee string together multiple reads can drag down efficiency. Against Florida on January 10, Tennessee scored only 67 and was outscored 41-28 in the first half after Florida sped up mistakes and took away easy second shots. Against Georgia on January 28, Tennessee still won 86-85, but the first-half shot profile was ugly: 11-of-35 overall and 2-of-11 from three before the Vols adjusted. Georgia’s switching length and bench pressure also produced a 32-10 bench-point edge and held Tennessee to just 3 points off turnovers despite 12 offensive boards by Tennessee’s starting frontcourt alone. Those are good examples that congestion and crowding ball handlers can flatten the initial action. ([utsports.com](https://utsports.com/news/2026/1/10/mens-basketball-21-22-vols-fall-on-the-road-at-florida))

Against pressure specifically, Tennessee’s season trend line says the Vols are much less comfortable when they lose the assist-to-turnover battle. In the official notes, Tennessee was 10-3 when posting the better assist/turnover ratio, but only 6-3 when the opponent did; likewise, they were 8-2 when their own A/TO was 1.5 or better and 8-4 when it fell below 1.5. That is actionable: extend full-court after makes, force Gillespie to give it up early, and then top-lock him on the return pass so Tennessee has to initiate through secondary handlers like Bishop Boswell or Amari Evans. ([utsports.com](https://utsports.com/documents/download/2026/2/5/G23_2-7-26_Kentucky.pdf))

Preferred pace: Tennessee is more comfortable in a controlled, physical game where possessions end with one shot for the opponent and two shots for them. The roster construction and statistical profile support that. They are elite on the offensive glass, defend the arc well, and do not rely on high 3-point volume. To force the opposite, you have to make the game a floor-balance game rather than a rebounding game: send guards back on the shot, run off every long rebound, and attack before Tennessee’s size gets set. Kentucky’s 74-71 win over Tennessee in Lexington on February 7 is a strong example. Tennessee led for 34:30, but Kentucky still won by scoring 44 paint points and 14 second-chance points while keeping Tennessee to 37.1 percent shooting in the second half and only 31 total rebounds. Tennessee did score 15 fast-break points, but Kentucky’s interior efficiency outweighed that. ([utsports.com](https://utsports.com/documents/download/2026/2/8/24_-_020726_-_Kentucky.pdf))

Size and athleticism mismatches are everywhere on this roster. At point guard, Gillespie is only 6-1 but owns a 6-5.25 wingspan, which helps Tennessee survive defensively against bigger guards. On the wing, Amari Evans is 6-5 with a 6-10.75 wingspan. Bishop Boswell gives them another long guard rebounder; he had 10 boards at Georgia. At forward, Nate Ament is 6-10 with a 7-1 wingspan and real shot-creation skill. DeWayne Brown II is 6-8 with a 7-3 wingspan. Inside, Felix Okpara is 6-11 with a 7-3 wingspan and a 9-4 standing reach, while J.P. Estrella is 6-11 with a 7-1.75 wingspan. Jaylen Carey is 6-8 with a 7-1.25 wingspan. Practically, that means smaller opponents are in trouble on the glass at the 3, 4, and 5, while slower centers can be run by Ament in space. The best matchup targets are Gillespie physically at the point of attack and whichever non-shooting big is on the floor offensively, because Tennessee can play two traditional rebounders together. ([utsports.com](https://utsports.com/documents/download/2025/11/10/G3_11-12-25_NorthFlorida.pdf))

On offense, Tennessee leans more team offense than pure isolation, based on the available distribution. Through 22 games, the Vols had 385 assists against 283 turnovers, and Gillespie alone had 119 assists. That is not an iso-only team. But the end-of-clock burden clearly tilts toward two players: Gillespie at 18.6 points and Ament at 17.1. Combined, they had 786 of Tennessee’s 1,809 points through 22 games, or 43.5 percent of the scoring. So while exact Synergy isolation frequency was not publicly accessible in primary sources I could verify, the evidence says Tennessee’s offense starts collectively but finishes disproportionately through Gillespie/Ament creation. Make those two work against length, switch late, and tag offensive rebounders hard. ([utsports.com](https://utsports.com/documents/download/2026/2/5/G23_2-7-26_Kentucky.pdf))

Transition offense and defense: the clearest game-level numbers available show Tennessee can run selectively, but it is not their primary identity. In the February 7 loss at Kentucky, Tennessee had 15 fast-break points to Kentucky’s 10. In the January 28 win at Georgia, Tennessee had 9 fast-break points while Georgia had 12. Those examples fit the broader profile: Tennessee will take transition chances, especially off Gillespie pushes and leak-outs by wings, but the bigger differentiator is second-chance scoring. Against Georgia, Tennessee posted 24 second-chance points off 26 offensive rebounds; against Kentucky in Lexington, the Vols were beaten despite leading most of the game because they allowed 44 paint points and did not dominate the rebound margin. ([utsports.com](https://utsports.com/documents/download/2026/2/8/24_-_020726_-_Kentucky.pdf))

Coaching adaptability is a definite yes. Rick Barnes’ staff has made visible in-game adjustments in multiple 2026 examples. Tennessee erased an 11-point first-half deficit to beat Texas A&M 87-82 in double overtime on January 13. Tennessee also came back from 42-31 down at halftime to nearly beat Kentucky on January 17, and the official notes list that game as a 10-point and 15-point comeback to win for Kentucky, meaning Tennessee had in fact flipped control after the break before losing late. Most clearly, at Georgia on January 28, Tennessee went from 31.4 percent shooting and 18.2 percent from three in the first half to 56.7 percent shooting and 66.7 percent from three in the second half. That is a real adjustment game, not random variance. Barnes teams do alter spacing, post usage, and who initiates after halftime. ([utsports.com](https://utsports.com/news/2026/1/13/mens-basketball-24-rv-vols-rally-to-beat-texas-am-87-82-in-double-overtime))

Concrete gameplan: To beat Tennessee you must do five specific things. First, gang rebound with numbers and prioritize hit-first box-outs on Okpara, Estrella, Carey, and Brown; if Tennessee gets 15-plus offensive boards, you are probably losing. Second, extend ball pressure on Gillespie and deny the return pass to force Boswell/Evans/Brown into extra decisions. Third, shrink the floor against Ament drives and make him finish through contact instead of catching on the move. Fourth, run after every long miss or live-ball turnover before Tennessee’s size gets set; do not let the game become a half-court wrestling match. Fifth, offensively attack Tennessee’s smaller lead guard with screening action, then force the help bigs to defend in space instead of camping near the rim. Florida’s turnover avalanche, Kentucky’s 44 paint points in Lexington, and Georgia’s first-half congestion all give a template. If you let Tennessee defend set possessions and own the glass, the Vols dictate terms. If you turn the game into a decision-speed game with clean defensive rebounding, they become much more beatable. ([utsports.com](https://utsports.com/news/2026/1/10/mens-basketball-21-22-vols-fall-on-the-road-at-florida))
